papers.title: Hole-doping induced ferromagnetism in 2D materials
papers.authors: Ruishen Meng, Lino da Costa Pereira, Jean-Pierre Locquet, Valeri Afanas’ev, Geoffrey Pourtois
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic materials are considered as promising candidates for the future generations of spintronic devices. Yet, 2D materials with intrinsic ferromagnetism are scarce. Hereby, high-throughput first-principles simulations are performed to screen 2D materials that present a non-magnetic to a ferromagnetic transition upon hole doping. A global evolutionary search is subsequently performed to identify alternative possible atomic structures of the eligible candidates, and 122 materials exhibiting a hole-doping induced ferromagnetism are identified. Their energetic and dynamic stability, as well as magnetic properties under hole doping are investigated systematically. Half of these 2D materials are metal halides, followed by chalcogenides, oxides, and nitrides, some of them having predicted Curie temperatures above 300 K. The exchange interactions responsible for the ferromagnetic order are also discussed. This work not only provides theoretical insights into hole-doped 2D ferromagnetic materials, but also enriches the family of 2D magnetic materials for possible spintronic applications.

papers.title: Antisite defect qubits in monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides
papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.

papers.title: Universal hydrogen-free synthesis and elemental doping of two-dimensional transition metal selenides
papers.authors: Ping Man, Lok Wing Wong, Ka Ho Leung, Zhiqiang Guan, Tianren Chen, Honglin Chen et al.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional transition metal selenides (TMSs) feature notable bandgap flexibility, versatile doping characteristics, and practical manufacturability, positioning them as promising candidates for next-generation electronics. However, their synthesis remains a critical bottleneck, as conventional chemical vapor deposition (CVD) routes require H2 assistance for selenization, raising safety, cost, and quality concerns and constraining elemental doping. Here we show a universal, H2-free CVD method that overcomes these limitations. Our approach produces a broad spectrum of 2D TMSs, including monolayer binaries, bilayer polytypes, alloys, and heterostructures, and is compatible with diverse substrates. Incorporating common metals (Al, Zn, Fe, Ni, Cu) into the precursor enhances growth kinetics and enables precise doping. Al-doped WSe2 exhibits markedly lower resistance, with centimeter-scale films attaining a hole mobility of 28.36 cm2 V−1 s−1 and an on/off ratio of 3.56×106, comparable to exfoliated and H2-assisted monolayers. This work establishes a safe, scalable, and tunable synthesis strategy for high-performance 2D electronics. 2D transition metal selenides (TMSs) exhibit interesting (opto-)electronic properties, but their bottom-up synthesis usually requires H2 gas, leading to safety concerns and cost implications. Here, the authors report a universal H2-free chemical vapour deposition method to grow large-scale metal-doped 2D TMSs on various substrates.

papers.title: What Is the Role of a Magnetic Mo Antisite Defect on Carrier Relaxation and Spin Dynamics in 2-D MoS<sub>2</sub>?
papers.authors: Chengan Lei, Zhao Qian, Yandong Ma, Rajeev Ahuja
papers.abstract: Antisite defects significantly influence the dynamic properties of monolayer MoS 2, yet the carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in spin-polarized Mo antisite-defective MoS 2 remain unclear. Understanding these processes is crucial for advancing optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices. Here, we employ first-principles calculations and ab initio nonadiabatic molecular dynamics with spin–orbit coupling (SOC) to explore carrier relaxation and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with a Mo antisite defect. This defect alters the material’s magnetic properties, leading to distinct relaxation behaviors: electron relaxation is slower than hole relaxation, and charge carriers in different spin channels exhibit varied dynamics. These differences arise from variations in electron–phonon coupling, SOC strength, and phonon mode activation. Our findings provide key insights into charge and spin dynamics in MoS 2 with magnetic defects and suggest strategies to enhance the performance of next-generation optoelectronic, spintronic, and valleytronic devices.

papers.authors: Jeng-Yuan Tsai, Jinbo Pan, Hsin Lin, Arun Bansil, Qimin Yan
papers.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Being atomically thin and amenable to external controls, two-dimensional (2D) materials offer a new paradigm for the realization of patterned qubit fabrication and operation at room temperature for quantum information sciences applications. Here we show that the antisite defect in 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can provide a controllable solid-state spin qubit system. Using high-throughput atomistic simulations, we identify several neutral antisite defects in TMDs that lie deep in the bulk band gap and host a paramagnetic triplet ground state. Our in-depth analysis reveals the presence of optical transitions and triplet-singlet intersystem crossing processes for fingerprinting these defect qubits. As an illustrative example, we discuss the initialization and readout principles of an antisite qubit in WS
                    2
                    , which is expected to be stable against interlayer interactions in a multilayer structure for qubit isolation and protection in future qubit-based devices. Our study opens a new pathway for creating scalable, room-temperature spin qubits in 2D TMDs.

news_articles.abstract: Various imperfections and impurities significantly degrade device performance by capturing and scattering the channel carriers. To suppress carrier scattering and improve transport properties, various chemical treatments have been explored to heal native defects and remove extrinsic impurities. In this study, we experimentally demonstrate that electrostatic injection of protons (H<sup>+</sup> ions) from an H-TFSI solution into tellurene effectively removes the gap states induced by Te vacancies. A defect-healing pathway employing protons was predicted via density functional theory (DFT) calculations. To experimentally realize this approach, we fabricated tellurene field-effect transistors encapsulated between top and bottom h-BN layers (approximately 15-30nm), which prevent direct contact between the H-TFSI solution and the tellurene channel while screening electrostatic interaction from residual TFSI⁻ ions. After proton injection into the Te channel through the h-BN gate dielectric layer, the counterclockwise transfer-curve hysteresis observed in pristine tellurene field effect transistors (Te-FETs) transfer curves reversed to the clockwise direction, accompanied by a substantial reduction in the hysteresis window. At room temperature, the protonated h–BN-encapsulated Te-FETs exhibit a field effect hole mobility of 345.47 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ and an on/off ratio of approximately 100, respectively.
news_articles.content_html:
Introduction

Two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors have been widely explored as channel materials for next-generation electronic devices [1]. The atomically thin geometry enables strong electrostatic gate control, which is essential for digital electronics [2]. In order to build energy-efficient two-dimensional logic circuits including inverters, NAND, and NOR gates, a complementary architecture is mandatory. Using only n-type field-effect transistors (FETs) for those applications leads to static power dissipation. A complementary p-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) FET is required to ensure power saving. Furthermore, optoelectronic applications strongly demand p-n junctions, which are fundamental to photovoltaic cells, light emitting diodes (LEDs), and photodetectors [3]. Among emerging 2D semiconductors, WSe2, black phosphorus (BP), and 2-dimensional trigonal tellurium known as tellurene (2D Te), are characterized as promising p-type materials [4].

Tellurene has recently re-emerged as a promising elemental 2D semiconductor [5]. The synthesis of tellurene is feasible through a hydrothermal method, enabling the growth of high-crystallinity flakes at relatively low temperatures [6]. Tellurene grows in 1D helical atomic chains with a certain handedness and then, self-assembly and van der Waals rafting of these atomic chains along the -axis form 2D layered sheets. It has a narrow band gap of approximately 0.35 eV in bulk form. However, through thickness control, the bandgap of tellurene can be increased to nearly 1.0 eV in the monolayer [7]. In addition, unlike BP, tellurene is air-stable. The lack of inversion symmetry and strong spin–orbit coupling further provide a fertile platform for exploring rich physical phenomena including chirality-dependent magnetoresistance [8], hedgehog-like spin textures [9], current-induced magnetization [10], superconductivity [11], and nonlinear Hall effects [12,13]. Owing to these structural and electronic characteristics, tellurene has been investigated for applications in electronics [6], optoelectronics [14], piezoelectric devices [15], thermoelectrics [16], spintronics [8], and quantum transport devices [17]. c

The p-type behavior of tellurene originates from the tellurium vacancies [18]. They act as carrier trap centers, resulting in mobility degradation and increased transfer curve hysteresis. In addition, because of the ionization of the vacancy site at room temperature, the on/off ratio of the channel current is small, weakening the gate modulation. Therefore, controlling these defect states is essential for improving the intrinsic transport performance of tellurene FETs.

Proton-based defect passivation offers a promising route for reducing bulk- and interface-related trap states in 2D semiconductor devices [19]. Most chemical passivation methods rely on the surface adsorption or slow diffusion of chemical agents, largely confining the healing effect to the surface. In some cases, penetration of the healing agent into the lower layers of the channel is sterically hindered by the large size of the healing molecules.

In this work, a theoretical investigation on vacancy healing in tellurene was carried out using density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The simulations reveal that the occupation of a single proton at the vacancy site is energetically most favorable with a high binding energy, whereas incorporation of a second proton is energetically unfavorable due to positive adsorption energy. The introduction of a single proton (H+) into the vacancy shifts the localized defect states into the conduction band continuum, effectively eliminating mid-gap trap levels. To validate this theoretical prediction, we experimentally introduced H+ ions from H-TFSI solution into hydrothermally synthesized tellurene. To achieve this, we fabricated an h-BN/Te/h-BN heterostructure FET, wherein Coulomb scattering of hole carriers by substrate impurities (SiO2) and chemical residues (TFSI- ions) is effectively eliminated. After the injection of the protons by applying the back gate bias, the off-conductance decreases by two orders of magnitude and the threshold voltage shifts negatively, indicating effective n-type doping and defect suppression. The field-effect carrier mobility is markedly enhanced, and the hysteresis window is substantially reduced. This study demonstrates that remote proton passivation effectively improves the transport performance of tellurene FETs, achieving a field-effect mobility of 345.47 cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Our remote passivation strategy leaves no chemical residues on the active channel and can be applied post-fabrication, overcoming the primary limitations of conventional chemical treatments.

Results and Discussions

Theoretical calculations on density of states of the protonated tellurene

In order to investigate the effect of Te vacancies and to explore the pathway to heal the defective lattice, we carried out theoretical simulations on the density of states (DOS) of tellurene using density functional theory (DFT) [Method]. Figure 1a presents the atomic structure and DOS of pristine trigonal tellurene with a defined handedness. The bandgap of monolayer tellurene is approximately 1.0 eV, and the Fermi level of intrinsic tellurene lies in the middle of the bandgap. When a Te monovacancy is introduced (Fig. 1b), the local atomic configuration around the vacancy is modified, and the atomic distance of Te–Te near the vacancy site relaxes from 2.78 Å in the pristine lattice to 2.65 Å. The formation of the vacancy generates deep in-gap defect states (indicated by the downward arrow in Fig. 1b). These defect states are located 0.27 eV above the valence band edge, donating hole carriers to tellurene. These deep-level states act as carrier trap sites and scattering centers via Coulomb interactions, degrading device performance.

To remove the gap states resulting from Te vacancies, we introduce protons into the vacancy site. The introduction of significantly modifies the defect states near the valence band, shifting them upward toward the conduction band edge. Ultimately, these defect states merge into the continuum states of the conduction band, eliminating the localized levels that trap and scatter hole carriers in the valence band. Because the vacancy cavity is significantly larger than a bare proton, the incorporation of additional protons was also examined. As shown in Fig. 1d, while the adsorption energy for the first proton is negative (favorable binding), the adsorption energy becomes positive upon introducing a second proton and increases steeply with further additions. Therefore, single-proton occupation of the Te vacancy is the thermodynamically favored configuration. Although all our experiment was conducted with 30-nm-thick tellurene samples, DFT calculations provide an insight for the healing of tellurene vacancies and device structure. H+

H-TFSI treatment and x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy

To insert protons into Te vacancies and evaluate their electronic effect, we employed bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide (H-TFSI, purum, >95%) [Method]. A droplet of the prepared H-TFSI solution was dispensed onto a tellurene FET and a negative back–gate bias was applied to drive H+ ions electrostatically into the tellurene, as shown in Fig. 2a. To confirm the incorporation of H+ ions into tellurene, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to characterize the Te 3d peak before and after the treatment with a 1 mM H-TFSI solution. Following H-TFSI treatment, the intrinsic Te⁰ 3d peaks show a clear shift toward higher binding energy. In pristine tellurene, the Te⁰ 3d₅/₂ and Te⁰ 3d₃/₂ peaks are located at 572.65 and 583.05 eV, respectively (Fig. 2b). After H-TFSI treatment, these peaks shift to 573.31 and 583.71 eV, upshifted by 0.65 eV (Fig. 2c). The blue shift of the Te⁰ peaks provides spectroscopic evidence for an n-type doping characteristic resulting from the introduction of the protons into defective tellurene. This observation is particularly noteworthy because the TFSI⁻ anion is widely recognized as a strong p-type dopant in various 2D semiconductors [20]. In contrast to the typical p-doping behavior of TFSI⁻, our H-TFSI treatment produces net n-type doping, fully consistent with our DFT calculations showing a Fermi-level upshift toward the conduction band. XPS also reveals an increase in surface oxidation (Te4+ components) from 10.44% to 22.02% after direct solution exposure. This surface oxidation is subsequently prevented through h-BN encapsulation. Although XPS cannot directly detect hydrogen due to its low photoionization cross-section, the observed n-doping and defect passivation are corroborated by electrical transport measurements.

Passivation of Tellurene on SiO2 substrate

To evaluate the electrical transport effects of H-TFSI treatment, we first characterized unencapsulated Te-FETs fabricated on 300 nm SiO2/Si substrates. The transfer characteristics of pristine Te-FETs show weak gate modulation with an on/off conductance ratio of only ~6 during dual gate sweeps (Fig. 3a). The transfer characteristics exhibit pronounced counterclockwise hysteresis. This hysteresis originates from both native Te vacancies in the channel and interface trap states on the SiO2 substrate. In p-type tellurene, hole transport dominates at negative gate voltages (Vgs = -60 V). The counterclockwise hysteresis loop from the pristine tellurene is primarily contributed to vacancy sites in tellurene via the following mechanism. At the onset of the up-sweep (Vgs = −60 V), the Fermi level shifts toward the valence band, resulting in the accumulation of hole carriers in the channel. Under this condition, a portion of the hole carriers is captured by Te vacancy sites, reducing the number of mobile holes participating in conduction. As the gate bias increases toward positive values, the trapped holes cannot be immediately released due to the slow response of the defect states. In contrast, at the onset of the down-sweep (Vgs = +60 V), the channel is depleted of hole carriers and the hole traps are expected to be largely emptied. As the gate bias decreases toward negative values, hole carriers accumulate in the channel, while their capture by the vacancy sites is delayed. Consequently, the channel conductance during the down-sweep remains higher than that during the up-sweep at the same gate bias, resulting in counterclockwise hysteresis.

To passivate these vacancies, an H-TFSI droplet was applied to the channel under a negative gate bias (Vgs = −80V) for 60 minutes. Following treatment, the on/off conductance ratio increased from 6 to 23 (Fig. 3a). While the on-state conductance increased by a factor of 1.7, the off-state conductance decreased by a factor of 2.7, reflecting vacancy passivation. Furthermore, the entire transfer curve shifted toward negative gate biases, confirming proton-induced n-type doping. However, the counterclockwise hysteresis direction remained unchanged, and the hysteresis window widened substantially.

This contrasting behavior suggests that hysteresis cannot be explained solely by the vacancy-related trap states in tellurene. Direct exposure of the channel to H-TFSI solution may introduce additional surface-related trapping centers associated with residual TFSI⁻ species. The enlarged counterclockwise hysteresis can be explained by the trapping and detrapping of hole carriers at TFSI⁻-associated trap states, as illustrated by processes 1–4 (Fig. 3c). At the beginning of the down-sweep, the positive gate bias depletes hole carriers in the channel, leaving the surface hole traps relatively unoccupied. As the gate bias decreases, hole carriers begin to accumulate in the channel (process 1). Further application of negative gate bias increases the hole concentration, while the delayed hole capture by surface trap states maintains relatively high conductance (process 2). Near the negative gate-bias limit, a portion of the accumulated holes can be captured by the surface trap states. During the subsequent up-sweep, the trapped holes are not immediately released, reducing the number of mobile carriers participating in conduction (process 3). As the gate bias further increases, electrostatic depletion and delayed hole emission maintain the reduced conductance (process 4). Consequently, the conductance during the up-sweep remains lower than that during the down-sweep, resulting in counterclockwise hysteresis. In addition, the tellurene channel is directly supported by the SiO₂ substrate, where interface trap states may also contribute to the hysteresis. Previous studies have demonstrated that proton injection from H-TFSI can passivate interface trap states at the MoS₂/SiO₂ interface [19]. A similar passivation effect may occur at the Te/SiO₂ interface during our treatment. If both Te vacancy traps and SiO₂ interface traps are suppressed by protonation, a reduction in the hysteresis window would be expected. Thus, the enlarged hysteresis suggests that additional trapping effects associated with residual TFSI⁻ species may outweigh the expected reduction in intrinsic and interface trap states. To minimize the interface trap sites and maximize the effect of proton-mediated vacancy healing, we employ hBN encapsulation of the tellurene channel.

Remote protonation and h-BN encapsulation

As noticed from XPS, the treatment of H-TFSI on tellurene produces the formation of tellurene oxides. Furthermore, residual TFSI- ions on Te channel works as trap centers of hole carriers. We expect that tellurene oxides and TFSI residues counteract the effect of vacancy healing by the protons, as evidenced from Fig. 3a. To resolve these issues, we fabricated a sandwich structure, in which the tellurene channel is encapsulated between bottom and top h-BN layers, schematically shown in Fig. 4(a). For the device, first, Au metal back gate electrode was deposited on a SiO₂ (300 nm)/Si (500 μm) substrate. Then, the bottom h−BN was transferred onto the gate electrode using a PDMS stamp. The thickness of the bottom h−BN gate dielectric is roughly 30 nm. Separately, tellurene was drop-casted onto a PDMS stamp, and the remaining liquid solvent was removed using N₂ gas blowing. The tellurene flake was subsequently transferred onto the bottom h−BN region. The thickness of Te ranges from 30 nm to 60 nm. After source and drain electrodes were deposited to contact the tellurene channel, top h−BN was transferred onto the device to complete the h−BN/Te/h−BN sandwich structure. The thickness of top h−BN gate dielectric is approximately 15 nm. The thickness of each device layer was confirmed using AFM, as shown in Fig. 4c. The h−BN dielectric is sufficiently thick to fully screen the coulomb interaction between the hole carriers and the ionic impurities from SiO2 and TFSI⁻ ions [21]. However, via natural diffusion, the protons may be unable to reach the bottom of the tellurene channel. For this reason, the negative back gate bias was applied to attract the protons under the conditions described previously.

After encapsulating tellurene using top and bottom h−BN gate dielectric, transfer curves of the h−BN passivated Te FET were characterized using dual gate sweeps. Prior to the H−TFSI treatment, the dual gate sweep results in a hysteresis curve, which is quite similar to what we observed from Te FET fabricated on SiO2 substrates, including counterclockwise hysteresis loop and low on/off ratio in Fig. 5(a). Thus, compared to Fig. 3(a), the persistent counterclockwise hysteresis is expected to originate from the defective Te, rather than the SiO2 substrate.

To scrutinize the effect of protonation of Te, a droplet of H-TFSI was placed on the 15 nm thick top h−BN gate dielectric and -9.6 V was applied between the Au back gate and H-TFSI for 60 minutes. After the proton injection, the droplet of TFSI was blown away using N2 gas. Then, the device was immediately transferred into a vacuum probe station for characterization.

Comparing the energy barrier for proton migration across bulk h−BN, ranging between 0.75 eV and 0.98 eV [22], because of our gate field strength, approximately 0.1 V/nm, which is in a similar field range required for the bidirectional transport of ions separated by two-dimensional materials [23], the top h−BN layer is expected to be permeable to H⁺ ions. Hence, the ions can easily reach not only Te, but also the bottom hBN layer under an applied gate field. Further evidence of treatment-induced charge transport through h−BN is provided by the gate leakage current measured across the 30 nm thick bottom h−BN dielectric, as shown in Fig. 5(b). Before H-TFSI treatment, the gate leakage current is nearly negligible, whereas it increases up to approximately 40 pA at Vgs = 10 V after treatment. The reversible gate current response is consistent with the possible redistribution of mobile protonic species within the hBN-based structure. Together with the hydrogen distribution observed by ToF-SIMS, these results support proton incorporation into the encapsulated heterostructure.

After H-TFSI treatment, the on/off conductance ratio of the h−BN-encapsulated Te-FET increases from approximately 5 to 70, nearly three times that of the treated Te-FET on SiO₂, as shown in Fig. 5(a). This improvement is mainly attributed to an order-of-magnitude reduction in off-state conductance, accompanied by an approximately twofold increase in on-state conductance. These changes are consistent with proton-mediated passivation of Te vacancy-related defect states. Furthermore, h−BN encapsulation separates the tellurene channel from residual TFSI⁻ species and the SiO₂ substrate, reducing extrinsic trapping and scattering effects and allowing the benefits of vacancy passivation to be more clearly observed.

After the treatment, in Fig. 5(a), the hysteresis window of the Te−FET remarkably reduces. If the Te is completely healed after the protonation, we should not expect any hysteresis. The conductance of Te is lower at down-sweep compared to the up-sweep, resulting in clockwise hysteresis that exhibits a stark contrast to Te devices before treatment. We attribute clockwise hysteresis to the ionic movement of mobile protons. Because the proton mass is several orders of magnitude larger than that of an electron, the ionic response to the gate field is substantially slower than the electronic response, preventing mobile protons from instantaneously following the gate voltage sweep. The proposed mechanism is illustrated by processes 1–4 in Fig. 5(c). At the beginning of the down-sweep, a positive gate bias drives mobile protons toward the interface between bottom h−BN and tellurene, where their positive charges deplete hole carriers in the p-type channel, resulting in low conductance (process 1). As the gate bias decreases toward negative values, the protons begin to migrate toward the bottom gate electrode. However, their delayed redistribution maintains the hole depletion effect, resulting in relatively low conductance during the down-sweep (process 2). Under sufficiently negative gate bias, the protons redistribute toward the bottom gate, reducing their electrostatic influence on the tellurene channel. During the subsequent up-sweep, the protons remain relatively close to the bottom gate, allowing the accumulated hole carriers to maintain high conductance (process 3). As the gate bias further increases toward positive values, the migration of protons back toward the h−BN/Te interface is delayed, maintaining higher hole conductance compared to the down-sweep (process 4). Consequently, the channel conductance during the up-sweep remains higher than that during the down-sweep at the same gate bias, resulting in clockwise hysteresis.

The carrier mobility (μ) of the protons inside crystalline bulk materials is extremely small, approximately μ = 3.86×10-9 cm2/V·s. In order to estimate the proton mobility, we adopt the diffusion constant D from a previous study [24]. Then, the constant was plugged into Einstein relation, for the evaluation of the proton mobility.

Considering the gate electric field of our device, approximately 0.1 V/nm, the traveling speed and time of the protons inside our device are expected to be approximately 38 μm/s and a few ms, respectively. Therefore, at high field, the protons have enough speed to catch up the gate sweep speed. However, at low gate field, the proton speed is low, so a slight delay is expected, which may be attributed to the clockwise hysteresis shown in Fig. 5(c). Nevertheless, the enhanced high on/off ratio is considered as the consequence of Te vacancy healing using the proton intercalation.

Conclusion

2D layered materials are always exposed to processes that introduce various imperfections and impurities from the synthesis to the device fabrication. For this reason, post-growth and -fabrication healing strategies have long been sought. Protons have the smallest ionic radius among chemical healing agents and exhibit high diffusivity in solid-state materials. Compared to the gas phases treatment that interact primarily with the top surface, the remote passivation using the protonation is more controllable and adaptable to the device because the solution can be cleanly removed post-treatment.

Method

DFT Calculations

In this study, Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations were conducted using the CASTEP module in Materials Studio to investigate the incorporation of H+ ions into Te vacancies. Norm-conserving pseudopotentials were utilized for their high precision and reliable transferability across varying dopant concentrations. The exchange-correlation potential was treated using the Generalized Gradient Approximation (GGA) formulated by Perdew, Burke, and Ernzerhof (PBE). A plane-wave kinetic energy cutoff of 720 eV was applied, with the self-consistent field energy convergence criterion set to 10-6 eV. To account for van der Waals forces and mitigate artificial interlayer interactions, the Grimme (DFT-D) dispersion correction was implemented. Furthermore, spin–orbit coupling (SOC) was enabled for pristine Te models to accurately simulate energy splitting. The Brillouin zone of the 3 × 3 × 1 Te supercell was sampled using a Gamma-centered 6 × 6 × 1 k-point mesh, ensuring the convergence of both electronic and ionic states. A 20 Å vacuum layer was introduced in the vertical direction to eliminate non-physical interactions between adjacent periodic images.

Synthesis of 2D Tellurene.

Sodium tellurite (Na2TeO3, 99%), ammonium hydroxide solution (ACS reagent, 28-30%), and hydrazine hydrate solution (80% solution in water, for synthesis) were purchased from Merck. Polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP, average M.W. 58,000) was obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. The precursor solution for 2D tellurene was prepared by dissolving sodium tellurite (0.1g) and PVP (0.5g) in deionized (DI) water (33 mL) with ammonia solution (4 mL) and hydrazine solution (2 mL). The solution was transferred into a Teflon-lined autoclave (100 mL volume) and then reacted at 180 ℃ for 10h. After the synthesis, glittering Te particles were found in the liquid. Mild centrifugation (3,000 rpm for 5 min) was conducted repeatedly with DI water to remove unreacted chemicals. After rinsing, Te flakes were dispersed in DI water and a droplet was spincoated on a target substrate.

Preparation of TFSI Solution.

We purchased bis(trifluoromethane)sulfonimide (H-TFSI, purum, >95%), and chlorobenzene (anhydrous, 99.8%) from Merck. To conduct the H-TFSI treatment for 2D tellurium, H-TFSI (0.0028g) was dissolved into chlorobenzene with continuous stirring for the preparation of 1 mM H-TFSI stock solution and the 0.01 mM of H-TFSI solution was prepared by the dilution of stock solution by 100 times. The H-TFSI decomposes to H+ and TFSI- ions. The process of solution preparation was performed in an N2 filled glove box due to the hygroscopicity of H-TFSI

Device Fabrication and Characterization

For the device fabrication, we used an e-beam lithography system (Post-Silicon Core-Facility Center of Sungkyunkwan University, NFEC-2019-06-256561) and an e-beam/thermal evaporation system (Post-Silicon Core-Facility Center of Sungkyunkwan University, NFEC-2013-05-178662). After the fabrication, the device was transferred to a closed-cycle refrigerator (Post-Silicon Core-Facility Center of Sungkyunkwan University, NFEC-2026-08-317577) for the characterization of electrical properties.

news_articles.abstract: The interface stability between garnet-type solid electrolytes (e.g., Li7La3Zr2O12, LLZO) and lithium metal anodes remains the primary bottleneck for next-generation solid-state batteries. We report a comprehensive high-throughput computational screening over 45 functionalized 2D transition metal carbonitrides (MXenes and MAB phases). By computing grand potential phase diagrams and interfacial reaction energies, we identify Ti3C2F2 and V2CTx as superior artificial SEI interlayers that effectively suppress lithium dendrite nucleation.
news_articles.content_html:
1. Background & Motivation

All-solid-state lithium metal batteries promise game-changing energy densities exceeding 500 Wh/kg. However, severe chemical side-reactions and dendrite propagation across the garnet electrolyte/lithium metal interface critically shorten cycle lifetime. In this study, we screen 2D transition metal carbides and nitrides (MXenes) to design an ultra-thin, chemo-mechanically robust artificial solid electrolyte interphase (SEI).

2. High-Throughput Computational Workflow

A Python-automated high-throughput DFT pipeline utilizing VASP and pymatgen screened 45 surface-terminated MXene compositions (M2X, M3X2, M4X3; M = Ti, V, Nb, Mo; Tx = O, F, OH, Cl). Li-ion diffusion pathways across the interfacial grain boundaries were evaluated using the climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method with 7 intermediate images.

3. Interfacial Stability & Lithium Diffusion Barriers

Among all candidates, fluorinated titanium carbide Ti3C2F2 demonstrated an ideal balance of low Li-ion migration barrier (0.22 eV) and thermodynamic passivity against metallic lithium reduction. The computed grand-potential phase diagram indicates complete electrochemical stability from 0.0 V to 2.4 V vs Li/Li+.

4. Summary & Outlook

Our findings establish atomic-level design guidelines for stabilizing solid-state lithium battery interfaces, paving the way for targeted experimental synthesis in the upcoming quarter.

news_articles.abstract: Accurate optical and quasiparticle band structures of single-layer transition metal dichalcogenides require treating many-body electron-electron and electron-hole interactions. Using state-of-the-art GW+BSE approaches implemented in VASP 6.3, we systematically analyze k-point convergence and screened Coulomb cutoffs for excitonic binding energies.
news_articles.content_html:
1. Introduction

Monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides host tightly bound excitons due to quantum confinement and reduced dielectric screening. We evaluate quasiparticle band gaps using single-shot G0W0 and partially self-consistent GW0.

2. Many-Body Computational Framework

Calculations were performed with a 24x24x1 Gamma-centered k-mesh and 480 empty bands, achieving exciton binding energy convergence within 15 meV.

3. Results

The computed A and B exciton peaks align with low-temperature photoluminescence measurements within 0.03 eV.
